title: Building Your Own OSS Project: Licensing & Foundations

tasks.title: Pick the License
tasks.why: For my own personal repo, write a justification in my journal: which license, and why (permissive vs copyleft, deliberately chosen). Add the LICENSE file, named exactly LICENSE, with year and copyright holder.

tasks.title: Hit 100% Community Profile
tasks.why: For one of my repos, complete every item on GitHub's Community Standards checklist: README, LICENSE, CONTRIBUTING, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, SECURITY, issue and PR templates. Screenshot the green page in my journal.

tasks.title: Write the CONTRIBUTING.md
tasks.why: Cover: dev environment setup, how to run tests, how to file a bug, my PR conventions, and my review expectations. This is what new contributors read first; if it's bad, I lose them.

tasks.title: Document Governance
tasks.why: Even as a solo BDFL, write a 1-page GOVERNANCE.md explaining how decisions are made. Implicit governance is the worst kind.

tasks.title: Audit a Real Project, Then Contribute
tasks.why: Pick an OSS project I actually use. Check its Community Profile, read its LICENSE, read its CONTRIBUTING.md. Then do one small, real thing: open a PR (typo fix, missing README example, doc clarification, anything genuinely useful).

tasks.title: Soft Skill: Setting Boundaries (Saying No)
tasks.why: Maintainer burnout is almost always an inability to say no. Practice the three kind, firm refusals: the clear no with rationale, the not-now no, and the boundary no. A maintainer who is still around in 3 years is the kindest thing a project can have.
